summary: Backdrop. The NIIP measures US-owned assets abroad minus foreign-owned assets in the US. Its change over time roughly equals the sum of four forces: the trade balance; capital gains or losses from asset-price and exchange-rate swings; a yield differential between US assets held abroad and foreign assets held in the US; and a net-position differential, whereby a larger liability stock grows faster than the asset stock for a given return. The US has long run persistent trade deficits yet avoided a proportionate NIIP decline, thanks to the "exorbitant privilege" â€” consistently higher returns on its foreign assets than foreigners earn on their US assets, concentrated in FDI.
